title: Jimmy Blanton's tuberculosis and death at Olive View
summary: A checkup on a lark revealed Blanton's tuberculosis; Lee drove him to sanitariums until he died at Olive View.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: because -- we discovered that he had tuberculosis by accident. We actually thought ... remember earlier when I told you we went up to Valverdi in the MGM thing?

Well, on the way up to Valverdi, we used to always try to outdress one another and say that we were better in sports than the other was, and we were always competing in everything. And so we were talking about how you are physically and all this, so we went to the doctor on the way to Valverdi, I mean, really on a lark -- just clowning.

And we went to the doctor to have a checkup. And it was really a lark, because I never did go to a doctor -- and so we went up there for about 4 days, and when we came back, the nurse came and she got me, you know, and she says, "Mr. Blanton, the doctor wants to see you." You know. And I said, "I'm not Blanton -- he's Blanton." She said, "Oh, Mr. Blanton, he wants to see you." So he thought it was me, and this was when he had found a spot on Blanton, and really, we always really attributed that to -- because he perspired freely, and he used to play -- they used to play Chicago and New York in the dead of winter, you know, and Bear just -- you know, he didn't change clothes. He would come out in that air; he was ringing wet after every show, and he'd stand outside and talk to people at the stage door, and like that, and I took
him to the sanitarium after he went away with Duke again, and he came back and he began to get ill.

I took him to 3 different sanitariums, put him in a blanket, and he was a good friend of Nat's, too, and the last time that we saw him, I had him at [Ollyview;] at first, I took him to the General Hospital, and you know, he said, he can't stay here because there was too much going on.

And I took him up and put him in a blanket, and put him in the back seat, because he was really small -- he had lost so much weight. I'll never forget, I picked Nat up one day at Adams & Hoover to go and see Blanton, and we got out there to see Blanton, and Blanton did not weigh 70 pounds then, you know, that's when we knew he was really going, when he was -- it was a terrible day for both of us, coming back.
You know, time takes care of all that, and people used to die from tuberculosis then, but you don't hear of it now. But he was a great musician.
Uh huh, yes, it was. Yeah.
